Corn___Common_Rust.description: Common rust is a fungal disease caused by Puccinia sorghi, causing powdery rust-colored pustules on leaf surfaces.
symptoms: Cinnamon-brown pustules on both upper and lower leaf surfaces.
Leaves turn yellow and may wither prematurely.
Pustules turn dark brown to black as the crop matures.
treatment: Apply recommended copper-based or triazole fungicides early in the season.
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation to keep the canopy dry.
Ensure proper crop spacing to improve ventilation.
prevention: Use rust-resistant hybrid corn seeds.
Practice proper crop rotation with non-host crops.
Maintain optimal soil health with balanced nitrogen application.

Corn___Gray_Leaf_Spot.description: Gray leaf spot is a fungal disease caused by Cercospora zeae-maydis. It causes rectangular lesions along the veins of corn leaves.
symptoms: Rectangular, gray-to-tan lesions restricted by leaf veins.
Lesions coalesce to kill entire leaf blades under hot and humid conditions.
Severe leaf blighting leading to stalk lodging and yield loss.
treatment: Apply strobilurin or triazole fungicides at the first sign of lesions.
Mow or till fields to accelerate the decomposition of residue.
Ensure balanced soil potash nutrition.
prevention: Select resistant hybrids with strong Gray Leaf Spot scores.
Practice a two-year crop rotation with soy or wheat.
Avoid no-till farming in fields with a history of the disease.

Corn___Healthy.description: The corn foliage is healthy, showing bright green leaves with no symptoms of fungal or bacterial infections.
symptoms: Leaves are vibrant green without any lesions or spots.
Firm stalks and normal grain development.
Uniform crop growth and dense canopy.
treatment: No active treatment required.
Continue standard irrigation and fertilizing routines.
prevention: Maintain periodic field scouting.
Follow balanced fertilizer application guidelines.
Avoid stress conditions like over or under-watering.

Corn___Northern_Leaf_Blight.description: Northern corn leaf blight (NCLB) is a destructive fungal disease caused by Exserohilum turcicum, producing large cigar-shaped lesions.
symptoms: Long, elliptical, cigar-shaped grayish-green or tan lesions.
Lesions appear first on lower leaves and move upwards.
Dirty green to dark gray dust-like spores on lesions during wet weather.
treatment: Spray triazole or strobilurin-based fungicides during silking.
Ensure thorough deep plowing of infected residue after harvest.
Incorporate crop rotation with soybean.
prevention: Plant NCLB-resistant corn hybrids.
Clean tillage tools before entering new fields.
Maintain optimal balanced plant nutrition.

Potato___Early_Blight.description: Early blight is caused by the fungus Alternaria solani. It affects leaves, stems, and tubers, producing dark target-like spots.
symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings (target board pattern) on older leaves.
Spots enlarge and cause leaf yellowing and dropping.
Leathery, sunken black spots on potato tubers.
treatment: Apply protectant fungicides like Mancozeb or Chlorothalonil.
Remove volunteer potato plants and nightshade weeds.
Apply organic mulch to reduce soil splash.
prevention: Use high-quality, certified disease-free seed tubers.
Ensure proper crop spacing and avoid overhead watering.
Rotate with non-solanaceous crops (e.g., corn, grass).

Potato___Healthy.description: The potato crop is healthy, showing vigorous green leaves and sturdy stems with no signs of blights or rot.
symptoms: Lush green, fully expanded leaves with no necrotic spots.
Sturdy upright stalks and healthy root systems.
Normal tuber skin coloration.
treatment: No treatment required.
Ensure proper hilling (mounding soil around plants) and uniform watering.
prevention: Scout fields weekly for symptoms.
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization late in the season.
Use clean irrigation water.

Potato___Late_Blight.description: Late blight is caused by the oomycete Phytophthora infestans. It is highly destructive and thrives in cool, wet weather.
symptoms: Dark, water-soaked lesions on leaves that expand rapidly.
White, fuzzy fungal growth on the underside of leaves in wet conditions.
Tubers develop brown-to-purple dry rot and decay quickly.
treatment: Spray systemic fungicides containing Metalaxyl or Dimethomorph immediately.
Destroy all infected crops and piles of discarded potatoes.
Harvest only in dry weather and store carefully.
prevention: Plant late blight-resistant potato cultivars.
Use certified disease-free seed potato tubers.
Ensure good soil cover (hilling) to protect developing tubers from spores.

Rice___Brown_Spot.description: Brown spot is a fungal disease caused by Bipolaris oryzae. It often targets crops growing in nutrient-deficient or poorly drained soils.
symptoms: Small, oval-to-circular brown lesions with yellow halos on leaves.
Large lesions dry up and cover the entire leaf blade.
Brown discoloration on rice grains leading to poor seed quality.
treatment: Apply trace element fertilizers (specifically zinc and potassium).
Spray fungicides like Propiconazole or Hexaconazole if severity increases.
Practice proper soil drainage to avoid waterlogging.
prevention: Use certified disease-resistant rice varieties.
Apply balanced NPK fertilization alongside micronutrients.
Keep fields weed-free to prevent spore transfer.

Rice___Healthy.description: The rice crop shows excellent vegetative growth, with erect green leaves and uniform plant height, indicating no symptoms of blast or leaf spots.
symptoms: Erect, uniform green leaf blades with no visible lesions.
Healthy root system in flooded or moist soils.
Normal panicle development during heading.
treatment: No treatment required.
Maintain consistent shallow flooding depth (2-5 cm) as per crop stage.
prevention: Monitor water quality and maintain proper NPK ratios.
Remove alternative grass hosts from field bunds.
Implement line planting for uniform light and aeration.

Rice___Leaf_Blast.description: Leaf blast is a highly critical fungal disease caused by Magnaporthe oryzae. It can lead to severe crop failure in susceptible varieties under humid conditions.
symptoms: Diamond-shaped (spindle) lesions on leaves with gray centers and brown borders.
Lesions enlarge and coalesce, burning or drying the leaves.
Lesions can also appear on the collar of leaves.
treatment: Apply systemic fungicides like Tricyclazole or Kasugamycin immediately.
Reduce nitrogen fertilizer application to limit disease spread.
Maintain continuous standing water in the field to buffer temperature.
prevention: Sow blast-resistant varieties like IR36 or local resistant hybrids.
Avoid late sowing to bypass optimal weather for fungal growth.
Use silicon-based amendments to strengthen plant resistance.

Rice___Neck_Blast.description: Neck blast occurs when Magnaporthe oryzae infects the neck node of the panicle, leading to broken necks and empty grain hulls.
symptoms: Grayish-brown lesions on the neck node of the panicle.
Neck rots and breaks, causing the panicle to fall over.
Grains fail to fill, appearing white, empty, and light.
treatment: Spray systemic fungicides like Tricyclazole or Isoprothiolane at late booting/early heading stage.
Harvest early if neck blast is widespread to save remaining grains.
Ensure fields are not dried out during flowering.
prevention: Avoid excessive nitrogen application at booting stage.
Use high-quality silicon amendments.
Practice thorough residue removal and field sterilization.

Sugarcane___Bacterial_Blight.description: Bacterial leaf blight of sugarcane is caused by Xanthomonas albilineans. It targets the vascular system of the cane, leading to leaf scalding and stalk death.
symptoms: Cream-to-yellow stripes on leaves parallel to veins.
Stripes turn reddish-brown and leaves wither from the tip.
Internal stalk tissue shows red vascular bundles when cut.
treatment: Use hot water treatment (50°C for 2 hours) on seed canes before planting.
Spray copper hydroxide bactericide to reduce surface bacteria.
Isolate and burn infected crop clumps immediately.
prevention: Plant disease-resistant sugarcane varieties.
Sanitize knives and harvesting tools with disinfectants between plants.
Improve field drainage to prevent bacterial transport in water.

Sugarcane___Healthy.description: The sugarcane stalks are robust and filled, foliage is dark green, with no signs of smut, red rot, or wilt.
symptoms: Wide, green, healthy leaves with clean midribs.
Thick, filled, and hard stalks with normal internode length.
Healthy root system and normal tillering.
treatment: No active treatment required.
Apply timely nitrogen and potassium fertilizers based on growth phase.
prevention: Practice regular earthing up to support cane weight.
Remove dry leaves (detrash) at 5th and 7th months to allow aeration.
Monitor for early pests like borers.

Sugarcane___Red_Rot.description: Red rot is caused by the fungus Colletotrichum falcatum. It is known as the 'cancer of sugarcane' and causes severe internal rot.
symptoms: Third or fourth leaf shows yellowing and dry margins.
Splitting the cane reveals internal red pith with white cross bands.
Characteristic alcoholic smell from affected split canes.
treatment: Uproot the entire infected clump, spray the spot with lime, and burn the residue.
Apply Trichoderma bio-fungicide to the soil.
Harvest the field immediately if infection is widespread.
prevention: Grow resistant varieties (like Co 86032 or local equivalents).
Practice crop rotation with rice or green manure crops.
Use healthy seed canes treated with bio-agents.

Wheat___Brown_Rust.description: Brown rust (leaf rust) is caused by Puccinia triticina. It is the most common wheat rust, forming small orange-brown pustules on leaf blades.
symptoms: Small, round, orange-brown pustules scattered randomly on leaves.
Pustules rub off as a brown powder (spores) on fingers.
Rapid defoliation under warm (15-25°C) and humid weather.
treatment: Spray propiconazole or tebuconazole fungicides at the first appearance of rust.
Ensure balanced potash nutrition to improve plant immunity.
Avoid high seeding density to reduce humidity inside canopy.
prevention: Cultivate resistant wheat varieties.
Sow early to avoid warm temperatures during grain filling.
Control volunteer wheat crops that carry the spores over summer.

Wheat___Healthy.description: The wheat crop is in excellent condition, leaves are uniform green with no powdery mildew or rust pustules.
symptoms: Uniform green leaf blades without yellowing or spots.
Strong erect stems and healthy green spikes.
No signs of wilting or head abnormalities.
treatment: No treatment required.
Ensure timely irrigation during critical stages like crown root initiation and flowering.
prevention: Maintain weed-free boundaries.
Apply nitrogen fertilizer in splits to prevent nitrogen stress.
Ensure proper crop rotation.

Wheat___Yellow_Rust.description: Yellow rust (stripe rust) is caused by Puccinia striiformis. It forms yellow stripes of pustules on leaves, thriving in cooler conditions.
symptoms: Yellow-to-orange pustules arranged in narrow, long stripes along leaf veins.
Affected leaf blades dry up and turn brown rapidly.
Stunted plant growth and shriveled grains.
treatment: Apply systemic fungicides such as Propiconazole or Triadimefon immediately.
Increase potassium fertilizer to support recovery.
Scout and isolate early infected patches.
prevention: Plant yellow rust-resistant wheat varieties.
Avoid late sowing to minimize exposure to cool humid conditions.
Ensure proper crop rotation.
